key_results: Chapter 1 (PDF pp. 25-31): discrete-time processing includes digital computation but also other sampled-data technologies; digital signals are discrete in both independent variable and amplitude, while discrete-time theory can be developed without assuming amplitude quantization.

Chapter 1 (PDF pp. 26-27): signal-processing objectives include producing a transformed signal, interpreting a signal to extract symbolic information, and manipulating signal-processing expressions; intelligent use of software still requires knowing what an algorithm computes and how to interpret it.
Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 34-36): a sequence is a function on the integers; x[n] is undefined, not zero, for noninteger n, and a sampled sequence alone contains no explicit sampling-rate information.

Sec. 2.1.1 (PDF pp. 36-41): every sequence can be expanded as a sum of scaled, shifted unit samples, x[n]=sum_k x[k] delta[n-k], providing the basis for the impulse-response representation of linear systems.

Sec. 2.1.1 (PDF pp. 39-41): discrete-time complex exponentials are identical when their frequencies differ by 2pi; a sinusoid is periodic only when omega0/(2pi) is rational, so higher normalized frequency need not mean shorter period.

Secs. 2.2.2-2.2.5 (PDF pp. 43-47): linearity is superposition, time invariance is commutation with an integer shift, causality excludes future input dependence, and BIBO stability requires every bounded input to yield a bounded output.

Sec. 2.3 (PDF pp. 47-53): a linear system's response to the impulse expansion is a superposition of responses to shifted impulses; for an LTI system this reduces to the convolution sum y[n]=sum_k x[k]h[n-k].

Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 53-59): discrete convolution is commutative, associative, and distributive; consequently LTI cascades commute and may be regrouped, and an inverse system has an impulse response whose convolution with h[n] is delta[n].
Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 56-59): an LTI system is causal iff h[n]=0 for n<0, BIBO stable iff h[n] is absolutely summable, and memoryless iff h[n]=K delta[n].

Sec. 2.5 (PDF pp. 59-65): a linear constant-coefficient difference equation does not define a unique output without auxiliary conditions; the initial-rest solution is LTI, recursive computation supplies causal solutions, and finite- versus infinite-duration impulse responses define FIR versus IIR systems.
Sec. 2.6.1 (PDF pp. 65-71): complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of every LTI system; input exp(j omega n) produces output H(exp(j omega)) exp(j omega n), where H is the DTFT of h[n].
Sec. 2.6.2 (PDF pp. 71-73): a causal system driven by a suddenly applied exponential generally produces a steady-state eigenfunction response plus a transient determined by the truncated convolution.

Sec. 2.7 (PDF pp. 73-80): the DTFT pair is X(exp(j omega))=sum_n x[n]exp(-j omega n) and x[n]=(1/2pi) integral over any 2pi interval of X(exp(j omega))exp(j omega n); the transform is periodic in omega with period 2pi.

Sec. 2.7 (PDF pp. 75-80): absolute summability is sufficient for a continuous DTFT, while finite-energy sequences may have mean-square convergent transforms with discontinuities; generalized transforms using impulses extend the representation further.

Sec. 2.8 (PDF pp. 80-83): a real sequence has a conjugate-symmetric DTFT; its real part and magnitude are even, and its imaginary part and phase are odd (subject to phase wrapping). Even/odd time decompositions map to real/imaginary spectral parts.

Secs. 2.9.5-2.9.7 (PDF pp. 85-89): Parseval equates sequence inner products/energy with spectral integrals; time convolution becomes spectral multiplication, while time multiplication (windowing) becomes periodic frequency convolution.
Sec. 2.10 (PDF pp. 90-95): an LTI system maps a wide-sense stationary input to a wide-sense stationary output; output power spectrum is |H(exp(j omega))|^2 times input power spectrum.

Sec. 2.10 (PDF pp. 94-95): for zero-mean white-noise input of variance sigma^2, input-output cross-correlation equals sigma^2 h[m] and the cross-power spectrum equals sigma^2 H(exp(j omega)), enabling empirical identification of an LTI system.

Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 119-130): the bilateral z-transform X(z)=sum_n x[n]z^-n becomes the DTFT on the unit circle only when that circle lies in its region of convergence; in polar form it is the DTFT of exponentially weighted x[n]r^-n.

Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 121-130): convergence depends only on |z|, so an ROC is an annulus centered at the origin; a rational transform must be specified together with its ROC because the same pole-zero expression can represent different right-, left-, or two-sided sequences.

Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 130-136): the ROC contains no poles and must be connected; a finite-duration sequence has the whole z-plane except possibly 0 or infinity, a right-sided sequence extends outside its outermost pole, a left-sided sequence extends inside its innermost pole, and a two-sided sequence occupies an annulus between poles.

Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 130-136): absolute DTFT convergence is equivalent to the unit circle lying in the z-transform ROC; for a rational causal LTI system, stability therefore requires every pole to be strictly inside the unit circle.

Sec. 3.3 (PDF pp. 136-144): inverse z-transforms can be obtained by inspection, partial fractions, or power-series expansion; the ROC determines which series/time support is valid and cannot be omitted.

Sec. 3.4 (PDF pp. 144-151): z-transform operations carry ROC qualifications: shifting can add/remove 0 or infinity, exponential multiplication scales/rotates poles and zeros, time reversal inverts the ROC, and convolution multiplies transforms with an ROC containing the intersection.
Sec. 3.4.8 (PDF p. 151): for a right-sided sequence that is zero for n<0, the initial-value theorem gives x[0]=lim_{z to infinity} X(z).

Secs. 4.1-4.2 (PDF pp. 165-175): periodic sampling x[n]=xc(nT) creates spectral replicas spaced by Omega_s=2pi/T and scaled by 1/T; normalized discrete frequency is omega=Omega T and contains no standalone record of T.

Sec. 4.2 (PDF pp. 169-172): the Nyquist sampling theorem states that a signal bandlimited to |Omega|<Omega_N is uniquely determined by periodic samples when Omega_s>2 Omega_N; overlap of replicas causes irreversible aliasing.

Sec. 4.3 (PDF pp. 175-178): ideal reconstruction lowpass-filters the sample impulse train and yields sinc interpolation, xc(t)=sum_n x[n] sin(pi(t-nT)/T)/(pi(t-nT)/T), exactly matching every sample and the entire bandlimited signal when sampling conditions hold.

Sec. 4.4.1 (PDF pp. 179-185): a C/D-LTI-D/C cascade is equivalent, for appropriately bandlimited inputs, to a continuous-time LTI system with effective response H_eff(j Omega)=H(exp(j Omega T)) for |Omega|<pi/T.

Sec. 4.4.1 (PDF pp. 179-183): an LTI discrete-time middle block alone does not guarantee a time-invariant continuous-time cascade; input bandlimiting or rejection of aliased components is also required.

Sec. 4.4.2 (PDF pp. 185-188): impulse invariance uses h[n]=T hc(nT) and maps Hc(j Omega) to H(exp(j omega)); it is exact for a prototype bandlimited below pi/T and otherwise introduces frequency-response aliasing.
Sec. 4.5 (PDF pp. 188-192): D/C-continuous-LTI-C/D realizes a discrete-time response H(exp(j omega))=Hc(j omega/T); this gives a meaningful implementation/interpretation of fractional-sample delay.

Sec. 4.6.1 (PDF pp. 192-197): downsampling by M retains x[nM] and produces (1/M) times the sum of M frequency-scaled spectral copies; alias-free decimation requires the input spectrum be zero for |omega|>pi/M, normally enforced by a prefilter.

Sec. 4.6.2 (PDF pp. 197-201): upsampling by L inserts L-1 zeros, replacing X(exp(j omega)) by X(exp(j omega L)); an interpolation lowpass filter of gain L and cutoff pi/L removes the images and fills the missing samples.

Sec. 4.6.2 (PDF pp. 200-201): linear interpolation has a triangular impulse response and appreciable imaging error when the source is only Nyquist sampled; it improves when the original is substantially oversampled.

Sec. 4.6.3 (PDF pp. 201-204): rational conversion L/M upsamples by L, filters with gain L and cutoff min(pi/L, pi/M), then downsamples by M; if M>L, the reduced output rate necessarily discards bandwidth to avoid aliasing.

Secs. 4.7.1-4.7.2 (PDF pp. 204-207): filtering may be moved across a downsampler/upsampler when its transfer function is correspondingly changed; the polyphase identity decomposes H(z) into M delayed components E_k(z^M).

Secs. 4.7.3-4.7.4 (PDF pp. 207-210): polyphase decimators compute filtering after rate reduction and interpolators avoid operations on inserted zeros; for an N-tap decimator the multiplication rate drops from N to about N/M per input-time unit.

Sec. 4.8.1 (PDF pp. 210-212): a practical anti-alias filter rolls off before pi/T; oversampling followed by a sharp digital decimator relaxes the analog filter, lowers analog cost, and can preserve phase with a linear-phase FIR.

Sec. 4.8.2 (PDF pp. 212-218): a practical A/D chain uses sample-and-hold, quantization, and coding; a B+1 bit uniform bipolar quantizer has 2^(B+1) levels, step size Delta=X_m/2^B, and clips outside its full-scale range.

Sec. 4.8.3 (PDF pp. 218-222): under the standard busy-signal model, rounding error is zero-mean white uniform noise on [-Delta/2, Delta/2] with variance Delta^2/12 and is uncorrelated with the input; the model fails for structured or coarsely quantized signals.

Sec. 4.8.3 (PDF pp. 221-222): quantization SNR improves by about 6 dB per added bit, but only when signal RMS is well matched to converter full scale; halving signal RMS with fixed full scale loses 6 dB.

Sec. 4.8.4 (PDF pp. 222-226): zero-order-hold D/A output is a staircase whose spectrum is multiplied by the hold response's sinc-like envelope; reconstruction/compensation filtering removes images and corrects passband droop.

Sec. 4.9.1 (PDF pp. 226-231): oversampling by M followed by ideal lowpass decimation leaves signal power unchanged but reduces in-band white quantization-noise power by M; every fourfold oversampling gains about one effective bit.

Sec. 4.9.2 (PDF pp. 231-235): first-order delta-sigma feedback leaves the signal transfer unity but shapes quantization error by 1-z^-1, giving noise PSD sigma_e^2[2 sin(omega/2)]^2 and moving most error out of the signal band.

Sec. 4.9.2 (PDF pp. 233-235): with first-order noise shaping, doubling the oversampling ratio gains about 1.5 effective bits rather than 0.5 bit for direct oversampling; pth-order shaping uses (1-z^-1)^p but higher feedback order increases instability risk.
Sec. 4.9.3 (PDF pp. 235-238): the reverse strategy improves D/A conversion: interpolate, requantize with shaped high-frequency noise, then use a simpler analog reconstruction filter.

For an LTI system, the output Fourier transform is the input transform multiplied by H(e^{jω}); |H| supplies frequency-dependent gain and the phase supplies frequency-dependent shift. Ideal brick-wall frequency-selective filters have infinite-duration, noncausal impulse responses, and adding linear phase merely shifts them. [§§5.1–5.1.1, printed pp. 241–242]

For a narrowband modulated signal, the carrier experiences the system phase while the envelope is delayed approximately by the group delay τ_g(ω)=−d arg H(e^{jω})/dω. Departure of group delay from a constant measures nonlinear phase distortion. [§5.1.2, Eq. 5.15, printed pp. 242–245]

A linear constant-coefficient difference equation becomes an algebraic rational system function in z. The same pole-zero expression can describe different impulse responses because the region of convergence is part of the system specification. [§§5.2 and 5.2.3, printed pp. 245–253]

For a rational causal system the ROC lies outside the outermost pole; stability requires that the ROC contain the unit circle. Causality and stability are therefore compatible only when every pole lies inside the unit circle. [§5.2.1, printed pp. 247–248]

An inverse system has system function 1/H(z). A causal stable inverse exists only when the original system has no zeros on or outside the unit circle; otherwise causality, stability, or both must be surrendered. [§5.2.2, printed pp. 248–250]

On the unit circle, log magnitudes, phases, and group delays contributed by factors in a pole-zero factorization add. A pole close to the unit circle produces a local magnitude peak, a nearby zero produces a dip, and a zero on the unit circle produces a null. [§§5.3.1–5.3.2, printed pp. 258–270]

The magnitude-squared function C(z)=H(z)H*(1/z*) has conjugate-reciprocal pole and zero pairs. Causality and stability select the pole locations for H(z), but reciprocal choices for zeros leave multiple stable causal systems with the same magnitude response and different phase. [§5.4, printed pp. 270–274]

A causal stable rational all-pass system pairs each pole inside the unit circle with a reciprocal-conjugate zero outside it. Its magnitude is unity at every frequency, while its continuous phase is nonpositive and its group delay is positive. [§5.5, printed pp. 274–280]

A minimum-phase system is causal and stable and has a causal stable inverse, equivalently all poles and zeros lie inside the unit circle. Any causal stable rational system can be factored into a minimum-phase factor and a causal stable all-pass factor without changing its magnitude response. [§§5.6–5.6.1, printed pp. 280–282]

Among causal stable systems with the same magnitude response, the minimum-phase member has the least phase lag, the least group delay, the largest initial sample magnitude, and the greatest partial energy accumulated up to every time index. Moving all zeros outside gives the corresponding maximum-energy-delay member. [§5.6.3, Eqs. 5.114–5.118, Figs. 5.30–5.32, printed pp. 287–291]

Generalized linear phase has H(e^{jω})=A(e^{jω})e^{−jωα+jβ}, where A is real and may change sign; phase jumps caused by the sign of A do not change the constant group delay α. [§5.7.2, Eqs. 5.135–5.137, printed pp. 295–297]

A causal FIR system has generalized linear phase when its finite impulse response is symmetric or antisymmetric. Symmetry and length parity produce four types: Type II is forced to zero at ω=π, Type III at ω=0 and π, and Type IV at ω=0, constraints that directly govern which response each type can approximate. [§5.7.3, printed pp. 297–308]

Equivalent block diagrams implement the same rational system in infinite precision but can behave very differently with finite register length. Structure is therefore an algorithmic and numerical choice, not merely a drawing convention. [§§6.1–6.3, printed pp. 341–354]

Direct Form I stores separate input and output histories and generally uses M+N delays. Reversing the pole and zero cascades lets the duplicate state chains collapse into Direct Form II, a canonical realization requiring max(M,N) delays, the minimum in general. [§§6.1 and 6.3.1, Figs. 6.3–6.7 and 6.14–6.17, printed pp. 344–356]

Factoring into first- and second-order sections yields cascade realizations with freedom to pair poles and zeros and order sections; partial-fraction expansion yields parallel realizations. These freedoms become design variables under quantization and internal dynamic-range constraints. [§§6.3.2–6.3.3, printed pp. 356–361]

The transposition theorem reverses every branch and interchanges input and output while preserving the transfer function, producing transposed direct, cascade, and parallel structures with different internal signals. [§6.4, printed pp. 363–366]

Symmetric or antisymmetric FIR coefficients permit folded linear-phase structures: equal coefficient pairs share additions and multipliers, roughly halving the number of multiplications while retaining exact generalized linear phase. [§6.5.3, printed pp. 368–370]

Coefficient quantization moves poles and zeros. IIR filters are especially sensitive when poles are clustered, repeated, or close to the unit circle; implementing quantized second-order sections in cascade gives more direct control than quantizing one high-order denominator polynomial. [§§6.7.1–6.7.3, printed pp. 377–384]

FIR coefficient quantization cannot destroy stability, but it perturbs zeros and the approximation error. Exact linear phase survives finite coefficient precision only if symmetric coefficient pairs are quantized identically. [§§6.7.4–6.7.6, printed pp. 384–391]

The standard linear round-off model replaces each quantizer by an additive source assumed wide-sense stationary, white, uniformly distributed over one quantization interval, and uncorrelated with signals and other sources. The text stresses that these assumptions are approximations most credible for complicated wideband inputs traversing many levels. [§6.8.1, Fig. 6.49, printed pp. 391–399]

In fixed-point IIR implementations, scaling internal nodes to avoid overflow reduces the available signal level and therefore worsens output signal-to-roundoff-noise ratio. Pole-zero pairing, section ordering, and where scaling is inserted determine the compromise. [§§6.8.2–6.8.3, printed pp. 399–410]

A direct-form FIR with independently quantized products injects M+1 noise sources, whereas accumulating full-precision products and quantizing only after the sum reduces the model to one quantization source. [§6.8.4, printed pp. 410–412]

Floating point greatly expands dynamic range and largely removes explicit scaling and overflow concerns, but requires exponent bits and more complex arithmetic; its error is relative to signal size, so the convenient fixed additive-noise model no longer applies directly. [§6.8.5, printed pp. 412–413]

Finite-precision feedback makes an IIR implementation nonlinear and can sustain zero-input limit cycles caused by product rounding/truncation or two’s-complement overflow. FIR systems cannot support such cycles: after the input becomes zero, an order-M FIR output is zero no later than M+1 samples afterward. [§6.9, printed pp. 413–418]

Impulse invariance samples a continuous-time impulse response. It maps an s-plane pole s_k to z=e^{s_kT_d} and preserves stability, but periodic spectral replication causes aliasing; it is useful mainly when the analog prototype is effectively bandlimited and is unsuitable without extra bandlimiting for highpass or bandstop designs. [§7.1.1, Eqs. 7.4–7.12, printed pp. 443–450]

The bilinear transform s=(2/T_d)(1−z^{−1})/(1+z^{−1}) maps the entire imaginary axis one-to-one onto the unit circle and the left half-plane inside it, eliminating aliasing. Its price is nonlinear frequency warping Ω=(2/T_d)tan(ω/2), handled by prewarping critical band edges. [§7.1.2, Eqs. 7.20–7.29, printed pp. 450–454]

Butterworth, Chebyshev I, Chebyshev II, and elliptic analog prototypes retain their monotone/equiripple magnitude character under the bilinear transform. Elliptic designs generally meet a magnitude specification at the lowest order, while every such rational design has nonlinear phase and the greatest group-delay variation near a band edge or transition. [§7.1.3, printed pp. 454–465]

Window-method FIR design multiplies an ideal infinite impulse response by a finite window, which convolves the desired frequency response with the window transform. Abrupt rectangular truncation narrows the transition as length grows but retains fixed-height Gibbs oscillation; tapering lowers sidelobes at the cost of a wider main lobe and transition. [§§7.2–7.2.1, Figs. 7.19–7.22, printed pp. 465–471]

Using a symmetric window on a symmetric or antisymmetric desired impulse response preserves generalized linear phase. The resulting amplitude is the periodic convolution of two real functions, separating the phase guarantee from the magnitude approximation. [§7.2.2, Eqs. 7.48–7.55, printed pp. 469–474]

The Kaiser window has independently adjustable length M+1 and shape β: increasing β suppresses sidelobes while widening the main lobe, and increasing M at fixed β narrows the main lobe without materially changing sidelobe height. Empirical formulas predict β and M from attenuation and transition width with little iteration. [§7.2.3, Eqs. 7.59–7.63, Fig. 7.24, printed pp. 474–478]

Window designs produce approximately equal peak passband and stopband ripple because both arise from integrating symmetric sidelobes. The transition width is controlled mainly by window length, while ripple is controlled mainly by window shape. [§7.2.4, printed p. 478]

Linear-phase type constraints matter in design: a Type-II highpass is forced to zero at ω=π and can fail badly even when length increases by one, while Type-IV differentiators avoid a Nyquist zero at the cost of a half-sample delay. [§§7.3.1–7.3.2, Figs. 7.26–7.30, printed pp. 479–485]

The FIR optimum-design problem is formulated as a weighted minimax polynomial approximation over disjoint passbands and stopbands, leaving transition regions unconstrained. For a degree-L approximation, the alternation theorem makes L+2 alternating extrema of equal weighted error necessary and sufficient for optimality. [§§7.4–7.4.2, printed pp. 486–498]

The Parks–McClellan algorithm uses a Remez-style exchange: solve on a proposed extremal set, locate the true error extrema, replace the set, and iterate until the maximum weighted error converges. The impulse response is recovered only after the optimum polynomial is found. [§7.4.3, Figs. 7.40–7.41, printed pp. 498–501]

For comparable equal-ripple specifications, the optimum equiripple design provides about 5 dB less approximation error than a Kaiser-window design of the same order, and unlike the window method it can assign unequal passband and stopband errors through weighting. [§7.4.4, Eq. 7.104 discussion, printed pp. 501–502]

There is no universally best IIR/FIR choice. IIR filters usually meet magnitude specifications at lower order and have closed-form prototype methods; FIR filters can provide exact generalized linear phase, arbitrary response shapes, unconditional stability, and stronger minimax optimality guarantees, with final choice depending on phase, arithmetic, hardware, software, and multirate context. [§7.6, printed pp. 510–511]

A period-N discrete-time sequence requires only N distinct harmonically related complex exponentials because frequency indices separated by N generate identical sequences. The DFS synthesis equation uses those N basis functions, and the analysis equation follows from their finite-sum orthogonality. [§8.1, Eqs. 8.1–8.12]

DFS coefficients and periodic sequences are both period N. Linearity, circular time shift, duality, conjugate/even/odd symmetries, and periodic convolution form the core algebra; periodic convolution in time corresponds to pointwise multiplication of DFS coefficients. [§§8.2.1–8.2.6, Table 8.1]

The Fourier transform of a periodic sequence is an impulse train in frequency whose weights are proportional to the sequence’s DFS coefficients; conversely, the DFS coefficients are equally spaced samples of the Fourier transform of one period. [§8.3, Eqs. 8.40–8.48]

Sampling X(e^{jω}) at N equally spaced frequencies, equivalently sampling X(z) at N equally spaced unit-circle points, produces a period-N sequence whose inverse DFS is the sum of time-shifted replicas Σ_r x[n−rN]. If the replicas overlap, frequency-domain undersampling appears as time-domain aliasing. [§8.4, Eqs. 8.49–8.57, Figs. 8.7–8.9]

The N-point DFT of a finite sequence is one period of the DFS coefficients of its periodic extension and is equal to samples of its DTFT/z-transform at z=e^{j2πk/N}; the inverse DFT reconstructs one period. The representation therefore carries an implicit periodicity even when the original sequence is treated as finite. [§8.5, Eqs. 8.58–8.68]

DFT properties are DFS properties interpreted on finite-length representatives: time shifts are circular, products correspond to circular convolution, and symmetry for real sequences permits one half of the spectrum to determine the other half. [§§8.6.1–8.6.6, Table 8.2]

The linear convolution of length-L and length-P sequences has maximum length L+P−1. An N-point circular convolution equals that linear convolution without time aliasing when N≥L+P−1; otherwise the excess tail wraps onto earlier samples. [§§8.7.1–8.7.2, Eqs. 8.129–8.139, Figs. 8.17–8.21]

An indefinitely long LTI filtering problem with a finite impulse response can be decomposed into blocks and evaluated by DFT multiplication using overlap-add or overlap-save, choosing transform length so circular convolution reproduces the required linear-convolution samples. [§8.7.3, Figs. 8.22–8.24]

DCT variants arise from different even periodic extensions of a real finite sequence. The DCT-1 corresponds to Type-1 symmetry with period 2N−2; the DCT-2 corresponds to half-sample Type-2 symmetry with period 2N. Both can be computed through related DFTs. [§§8.8.1–8.8.4, Eqs. 8.150–8.175, Figs. 8.25–8.26]

The DCT-2 often compacts correlated signal energy into low-index coefficients more strongly than the DFT, which is why it is central to transform coding. Symmetric extension also reduces objectionable endpoint discontinuities and blocking artifacts in image filtering. [§§8.8.5–8.8.6, Eqs. 8.176–8.180, Figs. 8.27–8.29]

Direct evaluation of an N-point complex DFT costs on the order of N² operations; FFT algorithms exploit twiddle-factor symmetry and periodicity by recursively decomposing the transform, reducing computation to order N log₂N for power-of-two lengths. [§§9.0–9.1]

The Goertzel algorithm evaluates a selected Fourier-transform/DFT value as the terminal output of a second-order real-coefficient recursion plus a final zero operation. Computing M selected values costs order NM and can beat a full FFT when M is smaller than roughly log₂N. [§9.2, Eqs. 9.4–9.9, Figs. 9.1–9.2]

Radix-2 decimation in time splits the input into even- and odd-indexed subsequences and recursively combines their DFTs with butterflies. There are log₂N stages; the unoptimized flow graph uses N log₂N complex multiplications/additions, with further savings from twiddle symmetry. [§9.3, Eqs. 9.10–9.19, Figs. 9.3–9.10]

Radix-2 decimation in frequency instead decomposes the output-frequency indices. DIT and DIF have comparable arithmetic but complementary ordering: common in-place forms place either input or output in bit-reversed order. [§§9.3.1–9.4.2, Figs. 9.11–9.24]

In-place butterflies overwrite arrays without losing needed data, reducing storage to N complex values; practical implementations must coordinate bit-reversed indexing, stage-dependent butterfly spacing, and coefficient access order. [§§9.3.1, 9.5.1–9.5.2]

Composite transform lengths can be factored into mixed-radix Cooley–Tukey decompositions; relatively prime factors enable prime-factor algorithms that exchange more complex indexing for fewer multiplications. [§9.5.3]

The Winograd Fourier transform rewrites short relatively-prime DFTs as periodic convolutions and can make multiplication count proportional to N rather than N log N, but its additions, bookkeeping, and separate multiplication/accumulation requirements can outweigh that benefit on general processors. [§9.6.1]

The chirp transform rewrites arbitrary equally spaced samples of a Fourier transform as a convolution between chirp-modulated data and a chirp impulse response. Its generalized chirp z-transform evaluates points equally spaced in angle on a spiral z-plane contour. [§9.6.2, Eqs. 9.37–9.52, Figs. 9.25–9.31]

In a fixed-point radix-2 FFT, an additive-noise model gives output noise power proportional to N before scaling. Scaling the input once to guarantee no overflow makes noise-to-signal ratio grow as N² (about one bit per stage); scaling by 1/2 at every stage improves the growth to N (about half a bit per stage). [§9.7, Eqs. 9.53–9.69, Figs. 9.32–9.36]

Block floating point normalizes the array, tests overflow during the FFT, shifts the whole array when necessary, and records a shared scale factor; floating point avoids forced stage scaling and makes noise growth with transform length substantially milder. [§9.7]

DFT-based Fourier analysis of a continuous signal comprises antialias filtering, sampling, finite windowing, and frequency sampling. For a sampling interval T and N-point DFT, bin k corresponds to continuous angular frequency 2πk/(NT), subject to periodic negative-frequency interpretation. [§10.1, Eqs. 10.1–10.5, Figs. 10.1–10.2]

Multiplying by a finite window convolves the true spectrum with the window spectrum. Main-lobe width controls the ability to resolve nearby sinusoids, while sidelobe level controls leakage; rectangular windows give narrow main lobes but high sidelobes, and Kaiser parameters explicitly trade length, main-lobe width, and sidelobe suppression. [§10.2.1, Eqs. 10.6–10.14, Figs. 10.3–10.4]

DFT spectral sampling can miss or misstate peaks that lie between bins. Zero-padding a fixed window increases the density of spectral samples and interpolates the same windowed spectrum but does not improve resolution; only increasing the observation/window length narrows the main lobe and resolves closer components. [§10.2.2, Examples 10.4–10.8, Figs. 10.5–10.10]

The time-dependent or short-time Fourier transform converts a sequence into a time–frequency function by transforming windowed neighborhoods. It is invertible when the window includes a nonzero reference sample and can equivalently be viewed as a bank of frequency-shifted versions of the window response. [§10.3, Eqs. 10.18–10.28, Figs. 10.11–10.14]

Short windows improve time localization but broaden the equivalent analysis filters; long windows improve frequency resolution but smear temporal change. With an L-sample window, N frequency samples and time hop R support exact reconstruction when the windowed blocks are fully represented and cover the signal (in the standard construction, N≥L and R≤L). [§§10.3.1–10.3.2, Eqs. 10.29–10.37, Figs. 10.13–10.16]

Overlap-add block convolution is a special use of the sampled time-dependent Fourier transform: modify each block spectrum by the filter response, inverse transform, then overlap and add reconstructed blocks. [§10.4, Eqs. 10.38–10.42]

Speech is locally stationary over roughly 30–40 ms: short-window wideband spectrograms reveal timing and vocal-tract formant motion, while long-window narrowband spectrograms resolve harmonic structure. [§10.5.1, Example 10.10, Figs. 10.17–10.18]

For pulse radar, round-trip delay estimates range and Doppler frequency estimates radial velocity. A short-time spectrum tracks changing Doppler peaks when motion is nonuniform, provided the window is short enough for local constant-frequency behavior but long enough to separate multiple returns. [§10.5.2, Eqs. 10.43–10.47, Fig. 10.19]

A (modified) periodogram is the normalized squared magnitude of the Fourier transform of a windowed record and equivalently the Fourier transform of its finite-record autocorrelation. It is nonnegative; after proper normalization it is asymptotically unbiased, but its variance remains approximately the square of the true spectrum, so it is not consistent. [§§10.6.1–10.6.2, Eqs. 10.48–10.66, Figs. 10.20–10.21]

Bartlett/Welch averaging divides a record into windowed segments and averages their periodograms. For K approximately independent segments, variance falls by 1/K; increasing segment length reduces bias but reduces K for a fixed record, creating a bias–variance/resolution tradeoff. Half-window overlap can nearly halve variance again, whereas heavier overlap yields diminishing returns. [§§10.6.3–10.6.4, Eqs. 10.67–10.77]

An alternative spectrum estimate first estimates autocorrelation, windows its reliable low-lag portion, and Fourier transforms it. Shorter lag windows smooth variance at the cost of resolution; nonnegative spectral estimates require a lag window whose Fourier transform is nonnegative. [§10.7, Eqs. 10.82–10.96]

The DFT computes the needed aperiodic autocorrelation by zero-padding a length-Q record and transforming |X[k]|²; to preserve lags 0 through M−1 without circular wrap, choose N≥Q+M−1. FFT evaluation typically becomes advantageous before M reaches about 100. [§10.7.1, Eqs. 10.97–10.99, Fig. 10.24]

A causal real sequence is completely recoverable from its even part; correspondingly, for a causal stable real sequence, either the real or (up to the value at zero) imaginary part of its Fourier transform determines the other through a periodic cotangent-kernel Cauchy-principal-value Hilbert transform. [§11.1, Eqs. 11.1–11.30, Figs. 11.1–11.2]

For an even-N finite sequence supported only through N/2, periodic causality creates finite-sum Hilbert relations between the real and imaginary parts of its DFT. The relations are circular convolutions and can themselves be evaluated efficiently with FFTs. [§11.2, Eqs. 11.31–11.52, Fig. 11.3]

If the complex cepstrum is causal—equivalently, for the minimum-phase case with all poles and zeros inside the unit circle—log magnitude and continuous phase form a Hilbert-transform pair. Magnitude determines phase; phase determines magnitude only up to an overall gain unless the cepstral zero term is known. [§11.3, Eqs. 11.53–11.56]

A discrete-time analytic signal has a spectrum zero on the negative-frequency half of each period. Its real and imaginary components are Hilbert-transform pairs: the ideal transformer has unit magnitude, phase −π/2 for positive frequencies and +π/2 for negative frequencies, and impulse response 2sin²(πn/2)/(πn) for n≠0. [§11.4, Eqs. 11.57–11.66, Figs. 11.4–11.6]

The ideal Hilbert transformer is noncausal and not absolutely summable. Window or equiripple FIR approximations preserve exact 90° phase plus linear delay: Type III has zeros at DC and Nyquist and many zero coefficients, while Type IV is zero only at DC and better covers the Nyquist neighborhood. [§11.4.1, Eqs. 11.67–11.70, Figs. 11.7–11.9]

A complex lowpass analytic signal shifted by e^{jω_cn} gives a one-sided complex bandpass signal. Its real part is an in-phase/quadrature representation and can be written as an amplitude envelope times a phase-modulated carrier, providing the standard basis for single-sideband modulation. [§11.4.2, Eqs. 11.71–11.77, Figs. 11.10–11.11]

A real bandpass signal can be converted to a complex analytic sequence, decimated without overlap according to its occupied bandwidth, processed at the reduced rate, then expanded, complex-bandpass filtered, and reduced to its real part for reconstruction. [§11.4.3, Eqs. 11.78–11.80, Figs. 11.12–11.13]

A discrete-time random process is an indexed family of random variables. Strict stationarity requires all joint distributions to be invariant to time shift; wide-sense stationarity requires constant mean and autocorrelation dependent only on lag. [Appendix A, §§A.1–A.2.1, Eqs. A.1–A.24]

For an ergodic process, infinite time averages of almost every sample sequence equal the corresponding ensemble mean and autocorrelation, motivating finite-record sample estimates. Statistical independence implies uncorrelatedness, but uncorrelatedness does not imply statistical independence. [Appendix A, §§A.2.1–A.2.2, Eqs. A.12–A.31]

Autocorrelation at zero equals mean-square value, autocovariance at zero equals variance, and correlation magnitudes are bounded by zero-lag powers. For many processes covariance decays to zero and correlation tends to the product of means with increasing lag. [Appendix A, §A.3, Eqs. A.32–A.42]

The power spectrum is the Fourier transform of autocorrelation; its integral gives average power, and it is real/nonnegative (and even for real processes). Through an LTI system, output power spectrum is |H(e^{jω})|² times input power spectrum. [Appendix A, §A.4, Eqs. A.43–A.55]

For rational systems driven by white noise, output average power can be obtained from the zero-lag inverse z-transform of σ²H(z)H*(1/z*), turning difficult real integrals or infinite impulse-response energy sums into partial-fraction calculations. [Appendix A, §A.5, Eqs. A.56–A.71]

Butterworth lowpass filters are maximally flat and monotonic; their 2N magnitude-squared poles lie equally spaced on an s-plane circle, and the stable causal filter selects the left-half-plane poles. [Appendix B, §B.1, Eqs. B.1–B.3, Figs. B.1–B.3]

Chebyshev Type I filters are equiripple in the passband and monotonic in the stopband; Type II reverses that allocation. Distributing allowable error uniformly generally meets a specification at lower order than the monotonic Butterworth approximation. [Appendix B, §B.2, Eqs. B.4–B.10, Figs. B.4–B.5]

Elliptic filters are equiripple in both passband and stopband and minimize transition width for a fixed order and ripple specification; achieving both ripples requires finite-frequency zeros as well as poles. [Appendix B, §B.3, Eq. B.11, Fig. B.6]
pedagogy: A rigorous, fundamentals-first DSP text that moves fluently among sequences, block diagrams, convolution, Fourier/DFT, z-plane geometry, probability, and implementation. Definitions are followed by explicit convergence conditions and algebraic derivations, then reinforced through paired time/frequency plots, pole-zero diagrams, flow graphs, numerical designs, and counterexamples that show where an attractive shortcut fails. The authors avoid unnecessary contour-integration machinery but expect advanced-calculus and complex-variable maturity; continuous-time LTI, Fourier, and Laplace foundations are prerequisites, while no prior discrete-time, z-transform, or DFT experience is assumed. Applications are introduced when they sharpen a principle—sampling converters, speech and radar spectrograms, filter structures, finite-word effects, FFT scaling, and quantization-noise experiments—rather than as a survey. A recurring teaching pattern is to derive an invariant in exact arithmetic, compare equivalent structures, then expose how causality, aliasing, finite precision, windowing, or computational cost changes the engineering choice. The exercise program is unusually substantial: hundreds of problems are stratified into basic-with-answers, further basic, and advanced work, mixing proofs, hand transforms and convolution, spectral/pole-zero sketches, flow-graph tracing, realization transformations, complete filter designs, numerical scaling, and computational investigations; Appendix C supplies answers to the first 20 basic problems in each chapter. MATLAB is encouraged after the analytic foundation is established, as reinforcement rather than a substitute for reasoning. Appendix A bridges the needed random-process theory and Appendix B summarizes analog prototype filters. The accessible artifact is explicitly the 1999 Second Edition by Alan V. Oppenheim and Ronald W. Schafer with John R. Buck; its scan-derived OCR is reliable for prose and structure, but equations and fine subscripts should be checked against the page images before verbatim reuse.

gems: Preface and Chapter 1 (PDF pp. 17-19, 28-29): the authors organize the book around the maxim that a fundamental text should 'uncover' rather than merely cover a subject, then connect fundamentals to intelligent use of MATLAB and future signal-processing environments.

Chapter 1 Historical Perspective (PDF pp. 29-31): Gauss is credited with discovering the FFT principle in 1805, before Fourier's harmonic-series publication, while the 1965 Cooley-Tukey disclosure is shown as the practical catalyst for modern DSP.
Example 2.2 (PDF p. 40): cos(pi n/4) has period 8, the higher-frequency cos(3pi n/8) has the longer period 16, and cos(n) is aperiodic—a compact demolition of continuous-time intuition.
Examples 2.6 and 2.8 (PDF pp. 44-45): the accumulator is used first to test linearity and then time invariance, turning an everyday recursion into a reusable systems-proof template.
Examples 2.12-2.13 (PDF pp. 50-53): convolution is computed both graphically and analytically, with piecewise overlap limits making the equivalence of the two methods explicit.

Examples 2.21-2.22 (PDF pp. 76-78): a causal exponential is absolutely summable, while the ideal lowpass impulse response is not absolutely summable but is square summable, sharply distinguishing transform convergence from energy convergence.

Sec. 2.10 (PDF pp. 94-95): driving an unknown LTI system with white noise makes its input-output cross-correlation proportional to the impulse response, an immediately lab-ready identification experiment.

Examples 3.1-3.5 (PDF pp. 123-127): one rational expression is repeatedly reused with exterior, interior, and annular ROCs, proving by construction that poles and zeros alone do not identify the time sequence.

Example 3.7 (PDF pp. 135-136): a single pole-zero diagram admits a stable two-sided realization or a causal unstable realization, but no stable causal realization; the unit circle and outermost pole make the contradiction visible.

Examples 4.1-4.3 (PDF pp. 172-174): a 2 kHz sinusoid sampled at 6 kHz, an 8 kHz sinusoid sampled at 6 kHz, and a 2 kHz sinusoid sampled at 1.5 kHz all produce the same normalized sequence cos(2pi n/3), while reconstructing to different analog aliases.

Sec. 4.3 (PDF pp. 175-178): every sinc kernel is one at its own sample time and zero at all other sample times; their weighted sum is both an exact interpolant and, under Nyquist conditions, the original signal everywhere.

Example 4.4 (PDF pp. 180-183): the same digital lowpass filter realizes different analog cutoff frequencies simply by changing T, making normalized-versus-physical frequency operational rather than notational.
Examples 4.5-4.6 (PDF pp. 183-185): an exact differentiator for bandlimited analog inputs is derived as a discrete filter and verified on a sinusoid through every transform-domain scaling step.
Example 4.9 (PDF pp. 189-190): a fractional-sample delay that has no literal index-shift meaning becomes intuitive as bandlimited D/C conversion, an ordinary continuous-time delay, and resampling.

Sec. 4.6.2 (PDF pp. 200-201): the text does not merely present linear interpolation; it plots its response against the ideal and explains why it is poor near Nyquist but reasonable for heavily oversampled signals.
Secs. 4.6.3-4.7 (PDF pp. 201-204): the concrete conversion T'=1.01T is implemented with L=100 and M=101, motivating why naive filtering at the huge intermediate rate demands multirate identities.

Secs. 4.7.3-4.7.4 (PDF pp. 207-210): polyphase decimation cuts an N-tap filter's multiplication rate from N to N/M per input-time unit, while interpolation avoids every multiplication by an inserted zero.

Sec. 4.8.1 (PDF pp. 210-213): speech intelligibility may need only 3-4 kHz although speech/noise extends toward 20 kHz; oversampling lets an inexpensive gentle analog filter hand sharp cutoff work to a linear-phase digital decimator.
Example 4.12 (PDF pp. 219-220): side-by-side 3-bit and 8-bit errors from x[n]=0.99 cos(n/10) show exactly when the white-noise quantization model is visibly implausible and when it becomes useful.

Sec. 4.8.3 (PDF pp. 221-222): the familiar 6 dB-per-bit rule is paired with the less-remembered warning that halving input RMS relative to fixed converter full scale loses the same 6 dB; roughly 16 bits are needed for 90-96 dB music reproduction under careful level matching.

Sec. 4.9.2 (PDF pp. 233-235): direct oversampling gains half a bit per doubling, first-order noise shaping gains 1.5 bits, and the p=2, M=64 table suggests nearly 13 extra bits—enough for a nominal 1-bit quantizer to approach 14-bit accuracy, subject to stability.

Example 5.1 turns group delay into a visible time-domain event: three adjacent narrowband pulses at 0.85π, 0.25π, and 0.5π enter together; the first is attenuated away, while delays of about 200 and 50 samples make the latter two emerge in reversed order. [§5.1.2, Figs. 5.1–5.3, printed pp. 243–245]

A pole-zero construction uses poles to build the lowpass passband and strategically placed zeros to suppress the stopband, making filter shape feel geometric rather than formulaic. [Example 5.10, Figs. 5.17–5.18, §5.3.2, printed pp. 267–270]

Four real causal FIR systems share exactly the same magnitude response but distribute their impulse-response energy differently; the minimum-phase version accumulates the most energy earliest and the maximum-phase version the least. [Figs. 5.30–5.32, §5.6.3, printed pp. 288–291]

The noninteger-delay construction interprets e^{−jωα} as samples of a shifted bandlimited interpolation even when α is not an integer—an unusually clean bridge from frequency-domain phase to fractional-sample delay. [§5.7.1, Fig. 5.33, printed pp. 292–293]

The four FIR linear-phase types make parity consequential: adding one tap can change the type, introduce or remove a forced Nyquist zero, and therefore improve or ruin a highpass approximation. [§§5.7.3 and 7.3.1, printed pp. 297–308 and 479–482]

In the chapter’s concrete realization, Direct Form II implements the same system as Direct Form I with two delays instead of three—the smallest possible state memory—by storing one shared internal sequence. [Example 6.2, Figs. 6.6–6.7, printed pp. 347–348]

The first-order finite-word example starts from a decaying stable system but rounding traps it forever at 1/8 for a=1/2, or in a ±1/8 period-two oscillation for a=−1/2. The quantizer has created dynamics absent from the ideal filter. [§6.9.1, Figs. 6.61–6.62, printed pp. 414–416]

A 4-bit two’s-complement second-order realization overflows into a full-scale period-two oscillation between +3/4 and −3/4 even with zero input; replacing wraparound by saturation prevents this class of overflow oscillation. [Example 6.14, §6.9.2, printed pp. 416–417]

The text connects the undesirable limit cycle to a useful device: when a periodic zero-input output is wanted, the same finite-word feedback behavior can serve as a digital sine-wave oscillator or generate DFT coefficients. [§6.9.1, printed p. 416]

The impulse-invariant sixth-order Butterworth example deliberately overdesigns the continuous-time stopband so that residual aliasing still leaves the digital result inside specification—a concrete example of budgeting transformation error rather than pretending it is absent. [Example 7.2, §7.1.1, printed pp. 446–449]

Applying the bilinear transform to an ideal linear phase produces a tangent-shaped phase, not another linear phase; the same transform that perfectly preserves stability and avoids aliasing can fundamentally distort delay. [Fig. 7.9, §7.1.2, printed pp. 453–454]

The rectangular-window discussion gives the sharpest statement of the Gibbs trap: making the window longer packs oscillations closer to a discontinuity but does not reduce their peak amplitude because the area under each shrinking lobe remains constant. [§7.2, Figs. 7.19–7.20, printed pp. 466–468]

Kaiser-window design turns trial-and-error into a short recipe. For the recurring lowpass specification, the empirical formulas produce β≈5.65 and M=37; increasing to M=38 produces a Type-I filter with peak error about 0.0008. [Example 7.8, Figs. 7.25–7.26, §7.2.3, printed pp. 476–478]

The Type-III versus Type-IV differentiator example makes half-sample delay a practical currency: the Type-IV design removes the forced Nyquist zero and extends the accurate amplitude range, but its delay is noninteger. [§7.3.2, Figs. 7.29–7.30, printed pp. 482–485]

For the same lowpass specification, the Kaiser-window method needs M=38, whereas weighted Parks–McClellan needs only M=27 because it spreads error equiripple and permits the stopband error to be one tenth the passband error. [§7.5.1, Figs. 7.43–7.44, printed pp. 503–506]

The order-26 and order-27 optimum lowpass filters each exhibit exactly fifteen alternations despite belonging to different linear-phase types; the order-26 filter just misses the specification, while order 27 meets it. [§7.5.1, Figs. 7.43–7.44, printed pp. 503–505]

A zero-order-hold correction is absorbed into the discrete-time filter by asking Parks–McClellan for a gently rising passband proportional to the inverse hold response; the compensated design costs only one extra order in the example. [§7.5.2, Figs. 7.45–7.46, printed pp. 506–507]

The multiband example is optimal by the alternation theorem yet develops nonmonotonic transition regions because those intervals are unconstrained—a memorable warning that mathematically optimal does not mean automatically acceptable everywhere. [§7.5.3, Fig. 7.47, printed pp. 507–510]

Time-domain aliasing is taught as the exact dual of ordinary sampling aliasing: the same nine-sample sequence is periodically replicated with N=12 (no overlap) and N=7 (overlap), making Fourier-transform undersampling visible without abstraction. [§8.4, Figs. 8.8–8.9]

Two identical length-6 constant sequences convolve linearly to an 11-point triangle; wrapping that triangle modulo 6 visibly produces the circular convolution, while N=12 leaves it intact. [Example 8.12, Figs. 8.18–8.21]

In the 32-point DCT energy-compaction example, approximation error stays very small until roughly 25 coefficients have been removed: the 32-number decaying sinusoid is represented with only seven DCT-2 coefficients and slight error. [Example 8.13, Figs. 8.27–8.29]
For N=1024, the chapter contrasts N²=1,048,576 with Nlog₂N=10,240 operations—more than a two-order-of-magnitude reduction before further twiddle simplifications. [§9.3, discussion after Fig. 9.7]
The FFT historical aside traces the underlying algorithm to Gauss in 1805 and notes that Cooley and Tukey’s 1965 paper turned a long-known NlogN idea into a signal-processing revolution. [§9.1]

The Goertzel-versus-FFT decision is made concrete: when only M frequency samples are wanted, direct/Goertzel work scales as NM and can win when M<log₂N, even though it loses badly when all N bins are required. [§9.2]
The chirp-transform example extracts just 16 Fourier samples, beginning at 2π/27 and spaced by 2π/1024, from a 26-sample sequence by one causal convolution. [Example 9.1, §9.6.2]

Fixed-point FFT scaling produces a memorable rule: input-only scaling costs about one extra bit of noise-to-signal ratio per stage, whereas distributing a factor of 1/2 at each stage costs about half a bit per stage. [§9.7, Eqs. 9.65 and 9.69]
A 5 kHz-sampled spectrum needing bins no more than 10 Hz apart requires N≥500, so a radix-2 implementation chooses N=512 and obtains 9.77 Hz spacing. [Example 10.1, §10.1]

The sinusoid sequence deliberately separates spectral sampling from resolution: padding a 32-sample window to a 1024-point DFT draws a smooth curve but cannot split merged peaks; lengthening the window while retaining N=1024 actually resolves them. [Examples 10.5–10.8, Figs. 10.6–10.10]

A Hamming-window spectrogram of a linear chirp uses a 400-sample window and turns the increasing instantaneous frequency into a straight dark trajectory across time-frequency space. [Example 10.9, Figs. 10.11–10.12]

The utterance ‘Two plus seven is less than ten’ is analyzed twice: a 6.7 ms Hamming window exposes temporal/vertical voicing structure, while a 45 ms window resolves harmonics but blurs transitions. [Example 10.10, Figs. 10.17–10.18]

Actual Doppler radar data show a strong peak curving through clutter; simply selecting the largest peak in each DFT tracks a trajectory consistent with a spinning rocket fin alternately moving toward and away from the antenna. [Example 10.11, Fig. 10.19]

Four pseudorandom white-noise periodograms with L=16, 64, 256, and 1024 become more rapidly jagged as L grows but never settle toward the flat true spectrum—the visual proof that the raw periodogram is not consistent. [§10.6.2, Fig. 10.20]
Welch’s half-window overlap nearly doubles the number of sections and almost halves estimator variance, but greater overlap stops helping because adjacent records cease to be independent. [§10.6.3]

The quantization-noise case study compares 8-bit and 3-bit quantization of the same speech: 8-bit error is nearly uncorrelated and within about −1.10 to +1.63 dB of flat after smoothing, while 3-bit error visibly follows the speech and its spectrum is unmistakably shaped. [§10.7.2, Figs. 10.26–10.30]

Increasing the 8-bit quantization record from 2,000 to 14,000 samples predicts a sevenfold variance reduction; the measured autocorrelation bounds tighten from roughly ±0.056 to about ±0.025, matching the theory. [§10.7.2, Figs. 10.27–10.28]

Two nearly equal Kaiser-window Hilbert designs expose a hardware tradeoff: the M=18 Type-III design needs only five multiplications per sample because alternate coefficients vanish, while the M=17 Type-IV design needs eight but covers frequencies near Nyquist. [Example 11.4, Figs. 11.7–11.8]

The bandpass-sampling construction fits M=5 shifted copies of a one-sided analytic spectrum into one 2π interval, enabling fivefold complex decimation without aliasing and subsequent exact reconstruction. [§11.4.3, Figs. 11.12–11.13]

Appendix A turns a difficult infinite sum or real frequency integral for second-order IIR output noise into a straightforward partial-fraction calculation of the zero-lag inverse z-transform, ending in a compact closed form. [Example A.2, Eqs. A.67–A.71]
